blocks.h: Why can `low` be updated before computing the profit?
p: On the day when `p` is the new minimum, `p - low` is 0 (buy and sell the same day), so it never beats `best` incorrectly. The sell day always comes after (or on) the buy day, since `low` only includes prices up to today.

blocks.h: Why is a single pass enough?
p: For each sell day the best buy day is simply the cheapest earlier day, and that is available as a running value.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(1).
Falling prices, e.g. `[7,6,4,3,1]`: every `p - low` is 0, so the answer stays 0.

121.takeaway: Single pass tracking the minimum so far: best profit = max(price − lowest earlier price).

blocks.h: Why start from the border instead of looking for surrounded regions?
p: 'Surrounded' is hard to check from the inside (a region can leak to the border through any cell). The opposite question is easy: an `O` is safe exactly when it is connected to a border `O`. So mark the safe ones, and everything else that is still `O` must be captured. In the example the group at (1,1), (1,2), (2,2) has no border contact and is captured, while the `O` at (3,1) is on the border and survives.

p: Without a marker, the last pass could not tell a safe `O` from a capturable one. The marker both prevents revisiting during the DFS and records the result.

bullets: Time: O(m·n) — each cell is marked at most once and checked a constant number of times.
Space: O(m·n) worst case for the recursion stack (the DFS can go as deep as the number of cells, which can also exceed Python's default recursion limit on large boards).

130.takeaway: Reverse the question: flood-fill from the border to find the safe O's, then flip everything else.

p: Square graph: 1–2, 1–4, 2–3, 3–4 (adjacency `1:[2,4]`, `2:[1,3]`, `3:[2,4]`, `4:[1,3]`). Each pop processes one original node:

blocks.h: Why a map from original to copy?
p: Graphs have cycles and shared neighbours. Without the map, you'd clone node 3 once from node 2 and again from node 4, creating two different copies, or loop forever around the cycle. The map guarantees one clone per original and lets any edge find the right clone in O(1).

blocks.h: Why register the clone before processing it?
p: `copies[nb]` is set when the neighbour is first seen, before it is popped. A node that is reached again via a different path (node 3 from 2 and from 4) is already in `copies` and just gets linked, not re-pushed.

bullets: Time: O(V + E) — each node is cloned once and each adjacency entry visited once.
Space: O(V) for the map and stack.

133.takeaway: Deep-copy a graph with a hash map from original to clone, which also serves as the visited set.

blocks.h: Why DP and not greedy matching?
p: Greedy can pick a word that blocks a later match. With `s = 'abcd'` and words `{a, abc, b, cd}`, always taking the longest match grabs `abc` and is left with `d`, but `a + b + cd` works. DP remembers *which prefixes are reachable* and tries all possible last words, so a failed greedy choice never hides a valid split.
The cheap boolean check runs first; the slice (a copy costing O(length)) and hash lookup happen only when the prefix up to `j` is splittable. This also prunes needless slices.

bullets: Time: O(n²) pairs (i, j) plus the cost of slicing/hashing each substring, so about O(n³) character work in the worst case.
Space: O(n) for `dp`, O(total word length) for the set.

139.takeaway: Prefix DP: dp[i] is true if some earlier true prefix j leaves s[j:i] as a dictionary word.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Hare; inside a cycle it must eventually land on `slow`
If the list ends, there is no cycle
`==` could compare values; two different nodes may hold equal values
Both pointers meet exactly where the cycle begins

p: List `3 → 2 → 0 → −4` with the tail linking back to `2`. Values shown are the node values the pointers sit on:

blocks.h: Why does restarting one pointer from the head find the entry?
p: Let `a` = steps from the head to the cycle entry, `c` = the cycle length, and `b` = steps from the entry to the meeting point. When they meet, slow has walked `a + b` and fast `2(a + b)`, so fast has gone around the cycle extra whole laps: `a + b = k·c`. Hence `a = k·c − b`, which is the number of steps from the meeting point forward to the entry (plus whole laps). A pointer from the head and one from the meeting point, both moving 1 step at a time, therefore arrive at the entry together. In the example the entry is the node with value 2.

bullets: Time: O(n) — slow makes at most about a + c steps before the meeting, and phase 2 takes at most a more.
Space: O(1).

142.takeaway: Floyd's tortoise and hare: detect the cycle with 1× and 2× pointers, then restart one from the head and move both by 1 to reach the entry.

rows: nums[mid] > nums[hi] → min is right of mid: lo = mid+1

p: Comparing `nums[mid]` with `nums[hi]` always reveals which side holds the drop: if mid is larger than hi, the drop (minimum) is right of mid; if smaller, the right part is sorted and the minimum is at or left of mid. Comparing with `lo` is ambiguous when the array isn't rotated at all.

If `nums[mid] == nums[hi]`, the value at `hi` also appears at `mid`, so even if `hi` is the minimum, a copy stays inside the range. Dropping `hi` never loses the minimum. Example: `[3,3,1,3]` (1): the tie at the start removes the last 3 and the search continues. This is also why the worst case, all elements equal, is O(n).

bullets: Time: O(log n) on average; O(n) worst case when many duplicates force `hi -= 1` repeatedly.
Space: O(1).

154.takeaway: Binary search comparing mid with hi; when equal, shrink hi by one — the cost of duplicates is a linear worst case.

p: A = `4→1→8→4→5`, B = `5→6→1→8→4→5`, where the tails share the nodes `8→4→5` (the `1`s in each list are different nodes). Values under each pointer after each step ('None' = fell off the end, then jumps to the other head):

blocks.h: Why does switching lists make them meet?
p: Let list A have `x` private nodes, list B have `y` private nodes, and `z` shared nodes. Pointer `a` walks `x + z` then `y`, pointer `b` walks `y + z` then `x`. After `x + y` steps both are at the start of the shared part. If there is no sharing (`z = 0`) they both reach `None` after `x + y` steps, so `a is b` is true with `None` and the loop ends returning `None`. The lengths' difference is cancelled with no need to compute lengths.

bullets: Time: O(m + n).
Space: O(1).

160.takeaway: Two pointers that switch to the other list at the end: both walk m + n steps, so they land on the intersection together (or on None together).

blocks.h: Why does a repeated remainder mean a repeating decimal?
p: The next digit depends only on the current remainder. If the same remainder shows up again, everything after it replays identically, so the digits written since its first appearance form the repeating block. `1 / 6` gives `0.1(6)` for the same reason: remainder 4 repeats after the 6.

blocks.h: Edge cases checked by running the code

bullets: Time: O(d) — there are at most d−1 distinct nonzero remainders, so the loop stops within d steps.
Space: O(d) for the map and digits.

166.takeaway: Long division with a remainder→position map: a repeated remainder marks the start of the repeating digits.

Vote for or against the candidate

blocks.h: Why does cancelling pairs find the majority?
p: Each time a non-candidate cancels a candidate vote, we remove one majority-element and one other element. The majority has more than half of all elements, so after all the pair-removals it cannot be fully cancelled: some copy remains. Note that the final `cand` is correct only because a majority is guaranteed; on `[1,2,3]` it would return 3, which isn't a majority. Without that guarantee you need a second pass to count `cand`.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(1).

169.takeaway: Boyer–Moore voting: the majority element survives pair-wise cancellation, so track one candidate and a counter.

head: Code

rows: Integer division: how many multiples of 5 (then 25, 125, …) are ≤ the original n
Each multiple of 5 contributes one factor, multiples of 25 a second one, and so on

p: `n = 25`: `n //= 5` gives 5 (multiples of 5 up to 25), then 1 (the multiple of 25), then 0. Answer: 6.

A trailing zero comes from a factor 10 = 2 × 5. In n! there are far more factors of 2 than of 5, so the 5s decide the count. Numbers like 25 contain two 5s (so they're counted once at the `//5` step and once at the `//25` step), 125 contains three, and so on. For n = 125 the loop adds 25 + 5 + 1 + 0 = 31.

bullets: Time: O(log n) — n is divided by 5 each time.
Space: O(1).

172.takeaway: Trailing zeros of n! = number of factors of 5: sum n//5 + n//25 + n//125 + …

blocks.h: Why exactly 32 iterations rather than 'while n'?
p: With `while n`, a number like 11 would stop after 4 bits and leave the reversed bits at the wrong place. Running all 32 pushes the leading zeros through too, so the lowest bit of `n` ends up as the highest bit of `res`. bullets: Time: O(1) — 32 iterations regardless of n.

p: Tree `[1,2,3,null,5,null,4]`:

blocks.h: Why 'last of each level' and not 'always go right'?
p: Following only right children fails when a right subtree is shorter than the left one: in this tree, level 2 holds `5` (under 2) and `4` (under 3), and the view shows `4` because it is the rightmost; but in a tree where node 3 had no children, the view at that level would be `5`, found only by looking at the whole level.

`deque([root])` with `root = None` creates a one-element queue holding `None`; `popleft()` returns `None` and `node.left` raises `AttributeError` (checked by running it). The problem statement allows an empty tree, so a guard like `deque([root] if root else [])` is safer than this code as written.

bullets: Time: O(n) — every node enqueued once.
Space: O(w) — the queue holds at most one level (the widest level).

199.takeaway: Level-order BFS keeping only the last node of each level — the rightmost node visible from the right.
